draft.title: Reading starlight with spectra
card: A spectrum is starlight spread out into its colours, like light through a prism. Dark or bright lines can appear in it.
Each element makes its own pattern of lines, like a fingerprint. Matching the lines in a star's spectrum to these patterns shows which elements the star contains.
The lines of a star can be shifted compared with the same lines measured in a laboratory. The size and direction of the shift shows how the star is moving.
This lets astronomers learn what a star is made of and how it is moving, even though it is too far away to visit.
draft.remember: The pattern of lines in a star's spectrum shows what it is made of, and a shift in them shows how it moves.

a.q: What does the pattern of lines in a star's spectrum tell astronomers?
opts: Which elements the star is made of
How many planets the star has
How old the star's light is
What colour the star's planets are
a.why: Each element gives its own pattern of lines, so the pattern shows which elements are in the star. The lines do not show planets, because they come from the elements in the star's light.
a.clue: Think of the lines as a fingerprint.

b.q: Astronomer Priya finds that a star's lines match those of hydrogen and helium, but sit in shifted positions. What can she conclude?
opts: It contains hydrogen and helium, and is moving
It contains only hydrogen, and is not moving
It contains neither element, and is moving
It contains hydrogen and helium, and is not moving
b.why: The matching patterns show hydrogen and helium are present. The shifted position of the lines shows the star is moving. The shift does not change which elements the lines point to.
b.clue: One feature shows content, the other shows motion.

a.best: Which elements the star is made of

b.best: It contains hydrogen and helium, and is moving
